profile.name: Perini Shivatandavam
profile.tagline: A vigorous, male-performed dance of warriors from Telangana, revived from Kakatiya-era traditions.
profile.insight: Revived by Nataraja Ramakrishna, this 'Dance of Warriors' was historically performed before the idol of Lord Shiva to invoke inspiration in soldiers departing for the battlefield.
profile.profile: Perini Shivatandavam is a vigorous dance form originating in Telangana, which reached its peak during the Kakatiya dynasty. Traditionally performed by men, it serves as a ritualistic invocation of Lord Shiva, intended to inspire warriors before they enter combat. The art form was reconstructed in the modern era through the study of ancient manuscripts and temple sculptures.
profile.profile_long: Perini Shivatandavam, also known as Perini Thandavam, is an ancient dance form from the Telangana region. It flourished during the rule of the Kakatiya dynasty, which established its center at Warangal and governed for nearly two centuries. The dance is historically documented in the Sanskrit text 'Nrttya Ratnavali' by Jayapa Senani and referenced in the 'Bhimeswara Puranam' by the poet Srinatha, where it is described as a dance offered as 'Ragabhoga' to Lord Bhimeswara at Draksharama. The dance is characterized by its vigorous nature and is performed to the resounding beats of drums. It is traditionally performed by men, who engage in the dance to reach a state of mental abstraction, seeking to channel the power of Lord Shiva within their own bodies. In ancient times, the dance was performed on special platforms in front of temples, specifically by warriors before they departed for the battlefield. Following the decline of the Kakatiya dynasty, the dance form nearly disappeared. In the modern era, Dr. Nataraja Ramakrishna initiated a renaissance of the art form by conducting extensive research into old manuscripts and analyzing the sculptures located near the Garbha Gudi of the Ramappa Temple in Warangal. Today, it is recognized as a revived tradition that maintains its connection to the martial and sacred history of the Kakatiya period.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance prospered during the Kakatiya dynasty in Warangal. It is mentioned in the Sanskrit text 'Nrttya Ratnavali' by Jayapa Senani and the 'Bhimeswara Puranam' by Srinatha. The form was revived in the modern era by Dr. Nataraja Ramakrishna through the study of manuscripts and temple sculptures.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed by males and is characterized as a vigorous movement style. Dancers aim to reach a state of mental abstraction to invoke the power of Lord Shiva. Specific footwork and gesture sequences are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is performed to the resounding beats of drums. No other specific instruments are described in sources.
sections.costume_and_setting: Historically performed on special platforms in front of temples. Sculptural evidence of the dance is found near the Garbha Gudi of the Ramappa Temple at Warangal.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance is performed in honor of Lord Shiva. It was traditionally enacted by warriors before leaving for the battlefield to invoke 'Prerana' (inspiration).
sections.notable_figures: Nataraja Ramakrishna (revivalist), Jayapa Senani (author of Nrttya Ratnavali), Srinatha (poet).
